newsitem.title: SPAIN: Clinton says he must await FBI probe on China.
newsitem.headline: Clinton says he must await FBI probe on China.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton said on Wednesday he would act in an "appropriate fashion" if it was found that China violated U.S. election laws, but said no conclusions should be made until an FBI probe had ended.
A U.S. Senate hearing began on Tuesday into possible violations of U.S. campaign funding with claims that China had tried to direct substantial sums of money to influence the 1996 American elections.
"I do not know whether it is true or not ... however it is a serious charge," Clinton said at a news conference at the end of a NATO summit.
Clinton also acknowledged that he mentioned the name of John Huang -- a central figure in the fundraising controversy -- to a Democratic Party official involved in raising political contributions.
Clinton has been hounded by allegations over his fundraising practices for his own re-election campaign in 1996 and for fellow Democratic candidates.

There has been repeated speculation that illegal contributions may have gone into Democratic campaign coffers from Chinese interests seeking more influence in Washington. The party has acknowledged that it received millions of dollars in questionable donations.
The issue has complicated Clinton's foreign policy moves, with U.S. officials not wanting their decisions suspected of being motivated by political considerations.

"If any country, any country, sought to influence policy through illegal means, including illegal campaign contributions to people running for president or people in the Congress, it would be wrong and a matter of serious concern," he said.
"But I simply don't know and I think we have to let the investigation (by the FBI) play itself out," he said.

"What I expect is the most vigorous possible investigation by the Justice Department and let's get the facts and when we get the facts we'll react in the appropriate fashion," Clinton said. The FBI is part of the Justice Department.

The Senate Governmental Affairs Committee chairman Fred Thompson, a Tennessee Republican, began the hearings by saying Senate committee investigators believe that high-level Chinese government officials crafted a plan to channel money to affect 1996 presidential and congressional elections.
China has bitterly denied such allegations, which first surfaced last year and prompted the FBI probe.
Clinton acknowledged that in 1995 he mentioned the name of former Commerce Department official Huang as someone interested in raising money for the Democratic Party.

"Most people don't volunteer to help you raise money in this world," Clinton said. "It's normally an onerous task. And so if anybody volunteered I would have referred virtually anybody's name to the party."
